Putnam 2025 & Lean tools

How should tools and verification feedback participate in mathematical reasoning?

My work

I built and iterated a proof execution loop and pi-lean-tools: Mathlib search, declaration and premise lookup, snippet checks, and local tactic trials. Exploratory tool feedback stays separate from final verification.

Result & scope

All 12 problems reached the internal final_verified criterion: 8 parallel attempts per problem, run sequentially by problem, with recorded times totaling about 5.5 hours. This is not an official Putnam result.

Methods & details

On A5, I compared runs with and without a natural-language-first instruction. Both settings produced proofs; without the instruction, the agent also chose to reason before formalizing. This single-problem comparison tests a design assumption, not a generally superior workflow.

Experiment design · tool development · run analysis
Team project · system & benchmarkFLT unfinished

ContextSwarm / FLTBench

When does a local result actually satisfy the needs of a larger formal proof?

My work

I analyzed proof progress against FLT dependencies, formulated a local-interface approach to long-horizon work, and contributed to prompts and tools. I diagnosed and drove a missing parent-route lookup through to team integration.

Result & scope

The team built a collaboration system and FLTBench with 10 layered Lean reconstruction tasks. A targeted check observed the agent obtaining the parent-use information after the interface change; the full FLT target remains unfinished.

Methods & details

My design memo starts with what an upper-level proof needs, lets subproblems emerge from actual gaps, and revisits how local results fit the larger proof. It informed prompt revisions that relaxed fixed checking and splitting requirements while retaining verification constraints.

I also worked on retrieval and segmented reading of FLTBench scaffold materials, and explored bidirectional links between shared research records (CPS) and multiple mathematical objects.

Same FLT project · analysis branchRetrospective analysis

Proof weaving: trace analysis

What can later agents actually build on, and what does the execution record establish?

My work

I analyzed selected traces and cases through proof objects, candidate versions, shared records, and verification events. Reconstruction uses the state available at the time of each event, rather than relations recorded later.

Result & scope

The team’s series of experiments totaled approximately 100B tokens and 40,000 aggregate agent-hours. My outputs include case materials, a diagnostic memo, visualizations, and manuscript revisions—not a claim of completed FLT.

Methods & details

I checked candidate revision, feedback delivery, and evidence of subsequent use separately. A repeated invalid candidate does not by itself show that feedback was received and ignored; retrieved records do not by themselves establish reuse.

The cases distinguish observed events, plausible mechanisms, and relationships that still need comparison or intervention. My contribution also includes proofreading and revisions.

Time-aware reconstruction · cases · visualizationRelated paper ↗
Mathematical modelingTechnical report

Collective acceleration

Can networked progress sharing shorten completion time when attempts may restart?

My work

I modeled individual advancement, progress resets, and maximum-progress synchronization between neighbors as a stochastic process. I derived the expected completion time for one agent and analyzed group completion under specific parameter and expander-graph conditions.

Result & scope

A conditional mathematical analysis—not a demonstrated scaling law for real language-model agents. The model does not represent persistent external records or version management.

Methods & details

The distinction matters: starting a new attempt does not necessarily erase earlier work. The model motivated further questions about how previous work is stored, retrieved, and continued.

Stochastic processes · graphs · completion time

04

Toward systems that improve their own ways of working

I want to combine system experiments with mathematical modeling to study autonomous exploration and sustained improvement at the level of the whole swarm—not only a fixed workflow or memory component.

01

Discover useful designs

How can a system identify and implement structural improvements, rather than only refine familiar components?

Tools, shared environments, information access, and organization remain possible objects of change.

02

Turn scale into capability

When do more computation and longer operation lead to better collective problem solving?

Compare complete resource costs and independent tasks; distinguish individual efficiency, parallel search, and genuine shared-task gains.

03

Improve the search for improvements

Can a system change how it generates, evaluates, and inherits modifications when its current approach stalls?

Explore multiple directions and test subsequent improvement ability, not just the best version obtained so far.

Proposed research, not an implemented self-evolving system. Formal mathematics is the starting point; other complex tasks remain part of the longer-term scope.

Explorations & notes

Personal exploration · July 2026

TacticWorld

I designed a data-collection scheme that executes several tactics from the same Lean state and records their consequences. The planned equal-budget comparison contrasts successful transitions alone with structured outcomes from multiple actions. Tooling and initial workflow exploration have begun; full training and comparative evaluation are not complete.

About

Mathematical structure. Systems. Experiments.

I am a Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence double-degree undergraduate at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. My interests in graphs, networks, and stochastic processes shape how I investigate dependencies, information flow, and collective behavior.

I enjoy building a system, watching what it actually does, and revising both the design and the questions. Unexpected behavior is often where the next useful experiment begins.
